stem:
A 31-year-old teaching assistant who is 14 weeks pregnant spent an hour in a small classroom with a pupil who was sent home because of a blistering rash that the school nurse thinks is chickenpox. She cannot remember whether she had chickenpox as a child and has never been vaccinated. She feels well and has no rash herself.

What is the most appropriate first step?

options.A: Check her immune status and seek urgent specialist advice
options.B: Give a live varicella vaccine today to protect her and the baby
options.C: Reassure her that no action is needed unless a rash appears
options.D: Prescribe an oral antibiotic to prevent bacterial superinfection
options.E: Offer counselling about termination because of the exposure

correct_answer: A. Check her immune status and seek urgent specialist advice
why_correct: A pregnant woman with significant contact and no reliable history of chickenpox needs her immunity established urgently, usually with a varicella-zoster IgG test, together with prompt specialist advice. If she is non-immune she can be offered post-exposure prophylaxis, an antiviral or varicella-zoster immunoglobulin, because chickenpox in pregnancy carries risks for both mother and fetus. Source: NICE CKS, Chickenpox: Scenario: Exposure to chickenpox, Last revised in November 2023.
why_wrong: B. Live vaccines are not given in pregnancy and a vaccine would not protect her in time after exposure. C. Waiting for a rash wastes the window in which prophylaxis can be given. D. Antibiotics have no role in preventing chickenpox. E. Exposure alone is not an indication for termination, and she may well be immune.
pearl: In pregnancy, significant chickenpox contact with unclear immunity means check varicella-zoster IgG and take urgent specialist advice, not wait and see.
thinking: Significant contact with probable chickenpox  ↓  Pregnant with uncertain chickenpox history  ↓  Establish immunity with varicella-zoster IgG  ↓  Urgent specialist advice on prophylaxis if non-immune
exam_trap: C, reassurance until a rash appears, tempts because she feels well, but prophylaxis must be given early and depends on knowing her immune status.
takeaway: Check immunity and seek specialist advice promptly after significant chickenpox contact in pregnancy.
notes: Same learning point as source (establish immunity, seek prompt advice) in a new school-contact vignette with live-vaccine, reassurance, antibiotic and termination distractors. Not a duplicate of live ID018 (IgG-negative woman, key is aciclovir prophylaxis) or PAAKT180/PAQ15264 (woman with a rash). Checked: CKS says seek urgent specialist advice and IgG testing may be done in primary care if results are available within 24-48 hours; the key does not depend on that window. Source item UN3337 treated as a within-batch repeat of this one.
Live duplicate: repeats live DR105 (tranexamic acid for heavy menstrual bleeding), OG056, DR104.

stem:
A 33-year-old woman has a positive home pregnancy test and her last period was about five weeks ago. She has had light brown spotting since yesterday but has no abdominal pain, shoulder-tip pain or dizziness and looks well. Two years ago she had a right tubal ectopic pregnancy treated with methotrexate.

What is the most appropriate next step?

options.A: Advise her to repeat the urine pregnancy test in about a week and return if bleeding continues
options.B: Reassure her and book routine antenatal care with the community midwife
options.C: Refer her to the early pregnancy assessment service because of her ectopic history
options.D: Prescribe a single dose of methotrexate in case the pregnancy is tubal
options.E: Start progesterone pessaries to reduce the chance of miscarriage

correct_answer: C. Refer her to the early pregnancy assessment service because of her ectopic history
why_correct: A previous ectopic pregnancy is a recognised risk factor for another, so this woman should have the pregnancy located by early assessment and ultrasound rather than being managed expectantly as a low-risk woman with early bleeding would be. Early pregnancy assessment services accept self-referral from women with a previous ectopic pregnancy. About a third of ectopic pregnancies occur in women with no risk factors, so the possibility must always be considered. Source: NICE NG126, Ectopic pregnancy and miscarriage: diagnosis and initial management, 2019 (updated 2026).
why_wrong: A. Watchful waiting with a repeat test is only for women with early bleeding and no risk factors such as a previous ectopic pregnancy. B. Routine booking would leave the pregnancy location unconfirmed and a possible ectopic pregnancy undiagnosed. D. Methotrexate is given only once an ectopic pregnancy has been confirmed. E. Progesterone does not address the main concern, which is excluding an ectopic pregnancy, and is not given before the pregnancy has been located.
pearl: A previous ectopic pregnancy raises the chance of another, so a new positive test with bleeding should prompt early assessment to locate the pregnancy.
thinking: Positive test with early spotting  ↓  Previous tubal ectopic pregnancy is a risk factor  ↓  Low-risk watchful waiting does not apply  ↓  Refer to the early pregnancy assessment service
exam_trap: A, repeat the urine test and wait, tempts because she is well and has no pain, but that advice is reserved for women without risk factors such as a previous ectopic pregnancy.
takeaway: Previous ectopic pregnancy means early scan and assessment in any new pregnancy.
notes: Source item was a recall of 'previous ectopic increases recurrence risk'; re-angled to the management decision that follows from the risk factor (NG126 rec 1.4.10 limits expectant management to women without risk factors such as previous ectopic; rec 1.3.3 self-referral). The stem gives 'about five weeks' only as scenario context; the key does not depend on a gestation threshold. No live item on this point (live ectopic items PAOG005, PAOG013, PAQ928, OG040, OG043 are diagnosis or treatment).

stem:
A 44-year-old woman has had light bleeding after sex on and off for three months, with occasional spotting between periods. Her last cervical screening result was normal. On speculum examination a soft, smooth, red, finger-like growth on a narrow stalk is seen emerging from the cervical canal. The rest of the cervix looks healthy and the uterus is normal in size on bimanual examination.

What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: A soft, smooth, red, finger-like growth arising from the endocervical canal is the typical appearance of a cervical polyp, a common benign cause of postcoital and intermenstrual bleeding. Polyps are usually removed in clinic and sent for histology. A cervix that looks consistent with cancer, which is not the case here, would need a suspected cancer pathway referral. Source: NICE NG12, Suspected cancer: recognition and referral, 2015 (updated 2026).
why_wrong: A. Ectropion is a flat red area of glandular epithelium around the os, not a growth projecting from the canal. B. Nabothian cysts are smooth, pale or yellowish retention cysts on the cervical surface and do not usually bleed. C. Cervical cancer typically gives an irregular, friable or ulcerated cervix rather than a smooth stalked growth on an otherwise healthy cervix. E. A prolapsed fibroid is usually larger and broader and is accompanied by an enlarged uterus.
pearl: A smooth stalked growth from the cervical os with bleeding after sex is a cervical polyp, but any cervix that looks suspicious still needs suspected cancer pathway referral.
thinking: Bleeding after sex and between periods  ↓  Visible smooth red stalked growth from the os  ↓  Rest of the cervix and uterus look normal  ↓  Cervical polyp
exam_trap: A, cervical ectropion, also causes bleeding after sex and tempts, but it is a flat red area on the cervical surface rather than a growth projecting from the canal.
takeaway: A smooth, soft, stalked growth from the os is a cervical polyp, a benign cause of postcoital bleeding.
notes: Source stem was a one-line recall item; built a speculum-finding vignette with ectropion, Nabothian cyst, cancer and prolapsed fibroid as distractors. Key checked against standard gynaecology teaching: no NHS/CKS page for cervical polyps was reachable (nhs.uk, patient.info, nhsinform URLs returned 404 or no content), so NICE NG12 rec 1.5.16 was opened only to support the point that a cancer-looking cervix needs suspected cancer pathway referral. Reviewer may wish to add an RCOG or BSCCP source. No live cervical polyp item found in the bank (live OG025, DF092, PAOG065, PAQ921 cover other postcoital bleeding points).
Live duplicate: repeats live OG007, OG042, PAQ895 (eclamptic seizure means IV magnesium sulfate).

stem:
A 27-year-old woman who is 18 weeks pregnant has had two days of stinging when she passes urine and needing to go more often. She has no fever, loin pain or vomiting, her observations are normal, and she has no drug allergies. A urine dipstick is positive for nitrites and leucocytes.

What is the most appropriate management?

options.A: Advise increased fluids and offer a back-up antibiotic prescription to use if symptoms persist
options.B: Send a midstream urine culture and start an antibiotic suitable in pregnancy now
options.C: Withhold antibiotics until the culture result is available, then treat
options.D: Prescribe antibiotics only if she develops a fever or loin pain
options.E: Advise cranberry juice and repeat the dipstick at her next antenatal visit

correct_answer: B. Send a midstream urine culture and start an antibiotic suitable in pregnancy now
why_correct: A pregnant woman with symptoms of a lower urinary tract infection should be offered an immediate antibiotic, with a midstream urine sample sent for culture before the first dose. Untreated infection can ascend to the kidneys and is associated with premature birth. The antibiotic is reviewed against the culture result, and nitrofurantoin, a usual first choice, is avoided at term. Source: NICE NG109, Urinary tract infection (lower): antimicrobial prescribing, 2018.
why_wrong: A. Back-up prescriptions and delayed treatment are for non-pregnant women, not for pregnancy. C. Waiting for the culture delays treatment in a woman at higher risk of complications. D. Waiting for a fever or loin pain means treating only once the infection may already have reached the kidneys. E. Cranberry juice and re-testing later do not treat an established infection.
pearl: Lower urinary tract infection in pregnancy is treated at once, after sending a urine culture, because of the risk of pyelonephritis and premature birth.
thinking: Dysuria and frequency with positive dipstick  ↓  Pregnant, so higher risk of ascending infection  ↓  Immediate antibiotic plus midstream urine culture  ↓  Review choice against sensitivities
exam_trap: A, a back-up prescription, tempts because it is standard for uncomplicated infection in non-pregnant women, but NICE advises immediate treatment in pregnancy.
takeaway: In pregnancy, treat symptomatic lower UTI immediately and send a urine culture.
notes: Source item was a 'why is prompt assessment important' reasoning question with a weak key; re-angled to a management decision testing the same principle (prompt treatment because of ascending infection and pregnancy complications). Key checked against NG109 recs 1.1.5-1.1.7 and table 2 (page shows no update date, published 31 October 2018). No live lower-UTI-in-pregnancy item found (live DS145 is pyelonephritis in pregnancy, a different decision).
Live duplicate: repeats live PAQ15263, PAQ15596, BX773, DS048, DS049 (rubella exposure in pregnancy).
HOLD: tautological (emergency contraception prevents pregnancy); emergency contraception covered by live OG033, OG047, BX283, BX501, PAOG073, PAN6003.
Live duplicate: repeats live BX989, BX872, OG057 (submucosal fibroid causes heavy menstrual bleeding).
